title: 09 — Choosing a Stack and a Build Plan
html:
09 — Choosing a Stack and a Build Plan

The one idea: pick the stack your team can run, keep the model behind an abstraction so you can switch, and build each kind of AI app in the same order: one working call, then grounding, then tools, then guardrails, then evaluation, then production.

1. Stacks

1.1 .NET and Azure

Layer Use (checked 2026-10-27)
Model access Official provider SDKs (for example the Anthropic C# SDK, dotnet add package Anthropic), behind Microsoft.Extensions.AI IChatClient so the provider can change
Agents and orchestration Microsoft Agent Framework (1.0 GA in 2026, successor to Semantic Kernel and AutoGen)
Hosting models Provider APIs. Claude is also offered on Microsoft Foundry. Azure-hosted models for in-region needs
Retrieval Azure AI Search, or a vector-capable database (PostgreSQL with pgvector, Azure SQL vector support)
Tools MCP servers with the official C# SDK (ModelContextProtocol), hosted in ASP.NET Core
Voice Azure AI Speech or Voice Live, or a LiveKit or Pipecat service alongside
Safety Azure AI Content Safety (including Prompt Shields), plus your own output handling
Secrets and identity Key Vault, managed identity, Entra ID
Observability OpenTelemetry to Application Insights

1.2 Python

Layer Use
Model access Provider SDKs (anthropic, and others)
Agents The SDK tool runner, Claude Agent SDK, LangGraph, or Microsoft Agent Framework for Python
Web API FastAPI with streaming responses
Retrieval Any vector database, or Databricks AI Search (OL 09)
Tools MCP Python SDK
Voice LiveKit Agents or Pipecat
Evaluation promptfoo, Ragas, DeepEval, MLflow

2. Reference build plans

Each plan is a sequence of working milestones. Don't start a step until the previous one works and is evaluated.

2.1 Knowledge chatbot (2 to 4 weeks)

  1. One call: a CLI that answers a question with a system prompt (02).
  2. Chat API: an ASP.NET Core or FastAPI endpoint with streaming, and a conversation store (03).
  3. Grounding: index approved documents with hybrid search, answer with citations, and an "I don't know" path.
  4. Handoff: create a ticket or transfer when not grounded or when asked.
  5. Safety: input checks, permission-aware retrieval, safe rendering (07).
  6. Evals: 50 or more cases across facts, refusals and safety, with a release gate (08).
  7. Production: auth, rate limits, tracing, dashboards, a feedback button.

2.2 MCP tool server (1 to 2 weeks)

  1. Pick three read-only tools with clear contracts (for example get_nav, list_schemes, get_factsheet).
  2. Build them with the official SDK over Streamable HTTP, statelessly (04).
  3. Test with the MCP Inspector, then from a desktop client and from your own agent.
  4. Add authentication, per-user permissions, rate limits and audit logs.
  5. Add evaluations: does the model pick the right tool, with the right arguments?

2.3 Agent (3 to 6 weeks)

  1. Prove the task needs an agent (section 1 of 05). Otherwise, build a workflow.
  2. Build the loop with an SDK tool runner and two or three tools.
  3. Add budgets, approval for side effects, and tracing.
  4. Evaluate on end-to-end task cases (success rate, steps, cost).
  5. Only then consider sub-agents, memory or a framework.

2.4 Voice assistant (3 to 6 weeks)

  1. Get a working chatbot first: the voice layer sits on top of it.
  2. Build a cascaded pipeline with LiveKit Agents or Pipecat, and streaming STT, LLM and TTS (06).
  3. Measure time to first audio, then tune end of turn and barge-in.
  4. Add telephony (SIP) if needed, plus consent, recording and retention rules.
  5. Evaluate on recorded test calls: task success, word error rate on key fields, interruptions.

3. Architecture for all four

---
title: One platform for chat, tools, agents and voice
---
flowchart TB
    subgraph CH["Channels"]
        WEB["Web and app chat"]
        TEAMS["Teams and WhatsApp"]
        PHONE["Phone and voice"]
    end
    CH --> GW["API gateway<br/>auth, rate limits, budgets"]
    GW --> ORCH["Orchestrator<br/>(chat service or agent)"]
    ORCH --> MODEL["Model behind an abstraction<br/>(IChatClient or provider SDK)"]
    ORCH --> RAG["Retrieval<br/>(permission-aware)"]
    ORCH --> MCP["MCP tool servers"]
    ORCH --> SAFE["Input and output checks"]
    ORCH --> OBS["Tracing, evals, feedback"]
    MCP --> SYS["Your systems and data"]

4. Code

There is no new code here. Each build plan links to the chapter with runnable examples.

5. Common mistakes

  1. Choosing a framework before writing one plain API call. Frameworks hide what's happening. Learn the raw calls first.
  2. Coupling the app to one provider's SDK everywhere. Put model access behind an interface.
  3. Skipping evals until the end. Build the eval set from day one.
  4. Building voice before the chatbot works. Voice multiplies every problem.
  5. No owner for prompts and tools. Version them like code, with review.

6. Exercise (1 hour)

Choose one of the four build plans for a made-up fund-services use case. Write a one-page plan: the stack you'd use and why, the first three milestones, your eval categories, and the risks from 07 that apply.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. Why put model access behind an abstraction such as IChatClient?
  2. What is the first milestone of every build plan?
  3. Why build the chatbot before the voice assistant?
  4. Which .NET framework replaces Semantic Kernel for new agent work?
  5. What makes an MCP tool server production-ready?

Answers

  1. To switch providers or models without rewriting the app, and to share middleware such as logging and caching.
  2. One plain, working model call.
  3. The voice layer sits on top of the same conversation logic and adds latency and turn-taking problems. Debug the logic first.
  4. Microsoft Agent Framework.
  5. Clear read-only tools, authentication with per-user permissions, rate limits, audit logs and tool-choice evaluations.

8. Sources

Checked 2026-10-27. See chapters 01 to 08 for the sources behind each choice.

  • Microsoft.Extensions.AI: https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/ai/microsoft-extensions-ai
  • Microsoft Agent Framework: https://learn.microsoft.com/agent-framework/
  • MCP C# SDK: https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/csharp-sdk
